passage:
Subject: is this normal??
Hi Avni Chechi,
Can I ask you something weird? Before your board results came out, did you keep asking your parents if it would be okay?
Because I do. Last night I asked Amma 'will I pass?' four times. Each time she said 'of course' and hugged me, and for about five minutes I felt fine. Then the worry came back, like a mosquito.
I also check the results website every hour even though the date is written clearly. I checked my roll number on the admit card six times today.
Appa finally said, 'Jomon, you already know what I'll say.' He's right. I do. I still need to hear it.
Does this ever stop?
Jomon

qa.q: How many times did Jomon ask Amma 'will I pass?' last night?
qa.a: Jomon asked Amma four times.

qa.q: Why does Jomon keep asking even after knowing the answer?
qa.a: Hearing it brings about five minutes of calm, and Jomon doesn't yet trust being able to handle the worry alone, so it keeps coming back like a mosquito.

qa.q: What turning point could help Jomon at this stage?
qa.a: Jomon could try sitting with the worry for a while instead of asking or checking, and Amma and Appa could kindly say 'you can handle this' rather than repeating the answer.

qa.q: What might Appa be feeling when he says 'you already know what I'll say'?
qa.a: Appa may feel tired and a little helpless, seeing that his reassurance doesn't last and wanting Jomon to trust what Jomon already knows.

grounding: It shows a teenager repeatedly asking parents for reassurance and checking the same worry, calmed only for minutes each time.

passage:
'Okay, Dolma, you asked why I'm always texting my mum. Here's the embarrassing truth.
Whenever she drives to work, I text "reached?" If she doesn't answer in ten minutes, I call. Then I call Papa to ask if he's heard from her. Then I check her location. When she finally replies "yes, reached 🙂", I feel amazing. For maybe twenty minutes.
Then there's the drive home in the evening, and it all starts again.
Last week she asked, really gently, "Sahil, what would happen if you waited?" And I realised I've never waited. Not once. I don't actually know if I can stand not knowing.
So now I'm trying one text only. No calls. It's horrible. But yesterday I lasted an hour, and nothing bad happened.'

qa.q: How long does Sahil wait before calling if Mum doesn't reply?
qa.a: Sahil waits ten minutes before calling.

qa.q: What did Sahil realise after Mum asked what would happen if Sahil waited?
qa.a: Sahil realised waiting had never once been tried, and felt unsure about being able to stand not knowing without her reply.

qa.q: Why is 'one text only, no calls' a useful turning point?
qa.a: It lets Sahil practise sitting with the worry instead of chasing quick relief, and lasting an hour shows the fear can be handled alone.

qa.q: How might Sahil's mum feel about the stream of texts and calls?
qa.a: She likely feels loved but also concerned, and her gentle question suggests she wants Sahil to feel safe without needing her constant replies.

grounding: It shows a teenager chasing reassurance through texts, calls and checking, feeling calm only briefly and never learning to cope alone.

passage:
Last winter, before my board exams, I must have asked Mummy the same question fifty times a day. "Will I pass? Are you sure? What if I blank out?" She'd say, "You'll be fine," and for about five minutes I'd feel okay. Then the worry would crawl back and I'd ask again, sometimes in the same sentence.
I also checked my admit card every night. Twice. Then once more after brushing my teeth. I messaged Imran: "Did you also study chapter 7? Are you sure it's in the syllabus?" He answered patiently, then less patiently.
The strange part is that every answer helped less than the one before. It was like drinking salt water. And somewhere deep down I started to believe I couldn't calm myself at all, that only someone else's "you'll be fine" could do it.
I'm Chinmay, and I didn't see the pattern until my mother gently stopped answering.

qa.q: How many times did Chinmay check the admit card each night?
qa.a: Twice. Then once more after brushing my teeth.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel after each reassurance?
qa.a: Chinmay felt calm for about five minutes, then anxious again, as each answer helped less than the last.

qa.q: What would help Chinmay more than more reassurance?
qa.a: Noticing the worry, sitting with it for a while without asking, and learning it can ease without someone else's answer.

qa.q: How might Imran feel answering the same questions?
qa.a: Imran likely feels patient at first, then tired and a little frustrated, unable to settle the worry for good.

grounding: A teen repeatedly asks for reassurance and rechecks worries, gaining brief relief but learning that the mind cannot cope alone.

School counsellor's note, 5 September
Aparna, Class 9, was referred by her class teacher, Ms Elizabeth, who noticed she asks the same question several times every period: "Is this going to be in the test? Are you sure?" Her mother told me on the phone that at home Aparna asks whether the door is locked, whether the gas is off and whether she will pass, up to twenty times an evening.
In our session Aparna said, "When someone says it's fine, I feel better. Then it starts again." She looked embarrassed. She said she hates asking but can't stop, and that she's scared she is "too weak to handle things on her own".
I explained that reassurance calms worry for a moment yet leaves the mind believing it always needs someone else. We agreed on an experiment: she will write the worry in a notebook and wait ten minutes before asking. Her mother will answer once, kindly, and then say, "You've got this."
Review in two weeks.

qa.q: Who referred Aparna to the counsellor?
qa.a: Her class teacher, Ms Elizabeth.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she said she's too weak to handle things alone?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious, stuck in a loop where each reassurance helps only briefly.

qa.q: What experiment did the counsellor suggest, and why?
qa.a: Writing the worry down and waiting ten minutes before asking, with one kind answer from her mother, so Aparna learns she can cope.

qa.q: What might Ms Elizabeth have noticed in class?
qa.a: She noticed Aparna asking the same question every period and felt concerned enough to refer her.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teen who asks the same worried questions again and again, easing fear briefly but learning she cannot cope alone.

passage:
Thursday night
I asked Jomon chettan five times today if the college fair next week will be okay. Five. He said yes every time. After the fifth he said, "Reena, you already know what I'll say."
I do. That's the stupid part. The moment he says it'll be fine, my chest loosens. For about three minutes. Then a new what-if pops up: what if I get lost, what if nobody talks to me, what if I say something weird. And I go back and ask again, just phrased differently.
At dinner Mummy said gently, "Molu, what do you think will happen?" I didn't want to answer. I wanted her to answer.
I think I've started to believe I can't calm down unless someone else does it for me. That scares me more than the fair does.
Going to try something: next time, count to fifty before asking. Just to see.

qa.q: How many times did Reena ask Jomon about the fair today?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What is Reena scared of, more than the fair?
qa.a: She is frightened that she can't calm down unless someone else does it for her.

qa.q: Why is Reena's plan to count to fifty a good start?
qa.a: It lets her sit with the worry a little and learn that it can ease without instant reassurance.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel after the fifth question?
qa.a: Jomon likely feels loving but tired, gently pointing out that Reena already knows the answer.

grounding: A teen keeps asking her brother for reassurance about an event, gets brief relief each time, and fears she cannot calm herself.

[Wednesday, 10:52 pm]
Kashish: bhaiya are you awake
Eshaan: ya. what happened
Kashish: will the results tomorrow be okay?
Eshaan: yes. you studied a lot 👍
Kashish: but what if I failed physics
Eshaan: you won't. you said the paper went fine
[11:14 pm]
Kashish: sorry. but are you SURE it'll be okay
Eshaan: Kashish. yes
Kashish: ok. ok. thanks
[11:40 pm]
Kashish: what if they put it online wrong
Kashish: bhaiya??
Eshaan: I've said yes 4 times. does it help?
Kashish: for like 5 min. then it comes back 😔
Eshaan: hmm. what if you tried to answer it yourself this time? what would you say to me?
Kashish: idk. that I studied. that even if physics is bad it's one subject
Eshaan: see. you know it. try saying that before you text me next time
Kashish: ok. will try. night

qa.q: How many times did Eshaan say he had said yes?
qa.a: Eshaan said he had said yes 4 times.

qa.q: What does Kashish mean when the reassurance helps for like 5 min?
qa.a: Kashish feels anxious and afraid, and the relief from being told it's fine fades fast, so the worry comes back and the checking starts again.

qa.q: What turning point does Eshaan offer, and why could it help?
qa.a: Eshaan asks Kashish to answer the worry alone, which shows Kashish can cope without constant reassurance; a parent or counsellor could help practise this too.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel after answering the same question again and again?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel tired and a little frustrated, but also caring, which is why he tries something different instead of refusing to reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager checking the same worry many times, with reassurance easing fear briefly while teaching the mind it cannot cope alone.
